method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom (whole-page renders plus glyph-level checks of every number and ambiguous token), with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry, caption, image and note. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch27 p837-840: auto-generated source checklist from existing 39 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 2x-3x zoom; any printed unit errors, ambiguous glyphs, or nonstandard expansions are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. No new medical facts introduced beyond the scan. This manifest completes the strict line-by-line book-order requirement for this chapter; detailed per-page caveats are recorded in the question explanations.

elements.source: The adrenal cortex constitutes what percentage of the adrenal gland? [The adrenal gland is 80% cortex and 20% medulla, situated on the kidney. (Book p837)]
The fetal : adult adrenal ratio is: [Fetal : adult adrenal ratio is 4:1. (Book p837)]
The adrenal primordium arises from: [At 6 weeks the urogenital ridge (a mesodermal derivative) gives the adrenal primordium (coelomic epithelium). (Book p837)]
Hormone synthesis in the developing adrenal begins at: [Hormone synthesis starts at 8 weeks of intra-uterine life. (Book p837)]
Urine formation begins at: [Note: urine formation begins at 9–10 weeks. (Book p837)]
Adrenal development is completed by: [Development is completed at 12 weeks; kidney development completes at 32–36 weeks. (Book p837)]
Kidney development is completed between: [Kidney development is completed by 32–36 weeks. (Book p837)]
The transcription factors listed for adrenal development are: [Transcription factors: SF-1, DAX1 (orphan receptors), WNT4. (Book p837)]

Match the suprarenal artery to its origin — 1) Superior suprarenal  2) Middle suprarenal  3) Inferior suprarenal … A) Direct branch of aorta  B) Renal artery branch  C) Inferior phrenic artery branch [Superior suprarenal = inferior phrenic branch; middle = direct aortic branch; inferior = renal artery branch. (Book p837)]

Match adrenal venous drainage — 1) Right adrenal vein  2) Left adrenal vein … A) Drains to left renal vein, then IVC  B) Drains directly to IVC [Right adrenal vein drains straight to the IVC; left adrenal vein drains to the left renal vein, then IVC. (Book p837)]

elements.source: Match adrenal relations — 1) Right gland anterior  2) Right gland posterior  3) Left gland anterior  4) Left gland posterior … A) Right crus of diaphragm  B) Stomach, pancreas, spleen  C) IVC and right liver lobe  D) Left crus of diaphragm [Right anterior: IVC + right liver lobe; right posterior: right crus; left anterior: stomach, pancreas, spleen; left posterior: left crus. (Book p838)]
The principal hormone of the fetal zone is: [The fetal zone's principal hormone in fetal life is DHEAS; the zone regresses after birth. (Book p838)]
‘The fetal zone of the adrenal cortex persists and enlarges after birth.’ [The fetal zone regresses after birth. (Book p838)]

Match definitive zone to hormone and regulator — 1) Zona glomerulosa  2) Zona fasciculata  3) Zona reticularis … A) Cortisol, pituitary  B) DHEAS, pituitary  C) Aldosterone, RAAS [ZG → aldosterone under RAAS; ZF → cortisol under pituitary; ZR → DHEAS under pituitary. (Book p838)]
The zona fasciculata contributes what share of the cortex? [Contributions: ZG 15%, ZF 75%, ZR 10%. (Book p838)]
Match zone to cortical contribution — 1) Zona glomerulosa  2) Zona fasciculata  3) Zona reticularis … A) 10%  B) 15%  C) 75% [ZG 15%, ZF 75%, ZR 10%. (Book p838)]
The zona reticularis forms by ___ of age (unlike the other zones, present at birth). [ZG and ZF are formed at birth; ZR forms by 2–3 years. (Book p838)]
Adrenarche — pubic and axillary hair growth from the zona reticularis — begins at: [Adrenarche occurs at 6–8 years and regresses post reproductive age. (Book p838)]
Maximum daily DHEAS production by the zona reticularis exceeds: [DHEAS is produced max daily >20 mg by the zona reticularis. (Book p838)]
On histology, the ‘large lipid-rich clear cells’ belong to the: [The zona fasciculata shows large lipid-rich clear cells. (Book p838)]

elements.source: StAR stands for ___, the rate-limiting step of steroid synthesis. [StAR = steroid acute regulatory protein; it is the rate-limiting step and its defect causes congenital lipid hyperplasia. (Book p839)]
StAR catalyses the first step, converting: [Cholesterol (LDL) enters via StAR to form pregnenolone. (Book p839)]
A neonate with pan-steroid deficiency is found to have a StAR defect. The named condition is: [The StAR defect (rate-limiting step) causes congenital lipid hyperplasia. (Book p839)]

Match the 17α-hydroxylase conversions — 1) Pregnenolone  2) Progesterone … A) 17OH-progesterone  B) 17OH-pregnenolone [17α-hydroxylase converts pregnenolone→17OH-pregnenolone and progesterone→17OH-progesterone. (Book p839)]
17,20 lyase converts 17OH-pregnenolone to: [17,20 lyase yields dehydroepiandrosterone from 17OH-pregnenolone (and androstenedione from 17OH-progesterone). (Book p839)]
3β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase converts pregnenolone to: [3β-HSD converts pregnenolone→progesterone (and the 17OH pair likewise). (Book p839)]

Match the 21α-hydroxylase substrates/products — 1) Progesterone  2) 17OH-progesterone … A) 11-Deoxycortisol  B) Deoxycorticosterone [21α-hydroxylase: progesterone→deoxycorticosterone; 17OH-progesterone→11-deoxycortisol. (Book p839)]

Match the 11β-hydroxylase conversions — 1) Deoxycorticosterone  2) 11-Deoxycortisol … A) Cortisol  B) Corticosterone [11β-hydroxylase: deoxycorticosterone→corticosterone; 11-deoxycortisol→cortisol. (Book p839)]

Match the aldosterone arm — 1) Corticosterone →(18-hydroxylase)  2) 18OH-corticosterone →(aldosterone synthase) … A) Aldosterone  B) 18OH-corticosterone [Corticosterone→18OH-corticosterone (18-hydroxylase) then →aldosterone (aldosterone synthase). (Book p839)]
Which enzymes are present ONLY in the zona glomerulosa? [The 18-hydroxylase/aldosterone synthase arm is only in ZG, explaining zone-specific aldosterone. (Book p839)]

Match gonadal enzymes — 1) Androstenedione→testosterone  2) Testosterone→DHT  3) Androstenedione→estrone … A) 5α-reductase type II  B) Aromatase (POR)  C) 17β-HSD type 3 [17β-HSD type 3 makes testosterone (and estradiol from estrone); 5α-reductase type II makes DHT (testis); aromatase (POR) makes estrone (ovary). (Book ]
In the pathway, POR stands for ___. [POR = P450 oxidoreductase; DHT = dihydrotestosterone; StAR = steroid acute regulatory protein. (Book p839)]

elements.source: The inherited form of 11β-OH steroid dehydrogenase type 2 defect is called: [Inherited 11β-HSD2 defect = apparent mineralocorticoid excess (AME). (Book p840)]
Normally, 11β-OH steroid dehydrogenase type 2 converts: [The enzyme converts cortisol (glucocorticoid + mineralocorticoid) to cortisone (glucocorticoid only). (Book p840)]

‘In AME the blocked cortisol→cortisone step causes excess cortisol, which then acts as a mineralocorticoid.’ [Blocking the conversion leaves excess cortisol driving mineralocorticoid effects (AME). (Book p840)]
The acquired causes of 11β-HSD2 inhibition listed are: [Acquired: Cushing's disease and licorice excess (inhibits 11β-OH steroid dehydrogenase type 2). (Book p840)]
‘Licorice excess produces hypertension by inhibiting 11β-OH steroid dehydrogenase type 2.’ [Licorice excess (−) inhibits 11β-HSD2, an acquired cause of the AME picture. (Book p840)]

A child presents with hypertension, hypokalaemia and alkalosis with salt + water retention but low aldosterone. The shared presentation triangle points to: [Both inherited and acquired 11β-HSD2 defects present with salt + H2O retention → HTN, alkalosis and hypokalaemia. (Book p840)]

Which is NOT part of the presentation triangle of 11β-HSD2 defects? [The triangle is hypertension, alkalosis and hypokalaemia (with salt + water retention); hyperkalaemia is the opposite. (Book p840)]
